entries.8bd8bbef6296b04ad3bfe4c5e8d610fe9177f371: <div sID="gen30547" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Rom.5" sID="Rom.5"/> <div eID="gen30547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30548" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30549" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having made good his point, and fully proved justification by faith, in this chapter proceeds in the explication, illustration, and application of that truth. I. He shows the fruits of justification, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.1-Rom.5.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. He shows the fountain and foundation of justification in the death of Jesus Christ, which he discourses of at large in the <reference osisRef="Rom.5.6-Rom.5.23">rest of the chapter</reference>.
entries.b040182c81346e16b19daff1b364e571a4e42d39: <div eID="gen30549" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30548" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Justification and Its Effects. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 58.)</title> <div sID="gen30550" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: <hi type="super">2</hi> By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. <hi type="super">3</hi> And not only <hi type="italic">so,</hi> but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; <hi type="super">4</hi> And patience, experience; and experience, hope: <hi type="super">5</hi> And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us. <div eID="gen30550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30551" type="x-p"/> The precious benefits and privileges which flow from justification are such as should quicken us all to give diligence to make it sure to ourselves that we are justified, and then to take the comfort it renders to us, and to do the duty it calls for from us. The fruits of this tree of life are exceedingly precious. <div eID="gen30551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30552" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">We have peace with God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.1">v. 1</reference>. It is sin that breeds the quarrel between us and God, creates not only a strangeness, but an enmity; the holy righteous God cannot in honour be at peace with a sinner while he continues under the guilt of sin. Justification takes away the guilt, and so makes way for peace. And such are the benignity and good-will of God to man that, immediately upon the removing of that obstacle, the peace is made. By faith we lay hold of God's arm and of his strength, and so are at peace, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.4-Isa.27.5">Isa. xxvii. 4, 5</reference>. There is more in this peace than barely a cessation of enmity, there is friendship and loving-kindness, for God is either the worst enemy or the best friend. Abraham, being justified by faith, was called <hi type="italic">the friend of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.23">Jam. ii. 23</reference>), which was his honour, but not his peculiar honour: Christ has called his disciples <hi type="italic">friends,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.13-John.15.15">John xv. 13-15</reference>. And surely a man needs no more to make him happy than to have God his friend! But this is <hi type="italic">through our Lord Jesus Christ</hi>—through him as the great peace-maker, <hi type="italic">the Mediator between God and man,</hi> that blessed Day's-man that has laid his hand upon us both. Adam, in innocency, had peace with God immediately; there needed no such mediator. But to guilty sinful man it is a very dreadful thing to think of God out of Christ; <hi type="italic">for he is our peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Eph. ii. 14</reference>, not only the maker, but the matter and maintainer, of our peace, <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col. i. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen30552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30553" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">We have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.2">v. 2</reference>. This is a further privilege, not only peace, but grace, that is, this favour. Observe, 1. The saints' happy state. It is a state of grace, God's loving-kindness to us and our conformity to God; he that hath God's love and God's likeness is in a state of grace. Now into this grace we have access <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">prosagogen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">an introduction,</hi> which implies that we were not born in this state; we are <hi type="italic">by nature children of wrath,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the carnal mind is enmity against God;</hi> but we are brought into it. We could not have got into it of ourselves, nor have conquered the difficulties in the way, but we have a manuduction, a leading by the hand,—are led into it as blind, or lame, or weak people are led,—are introduced as pardoned offenders,—are introduced by some favourite at court to kiss the king's hand, as strangers, that are to have audience, are conducted. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Prosagogen eschekamen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">We have had access.</hi> He speaks of those that have been already brought out of a state of nature into a state of grace. Paul, in his conversion, had this access; then he was made nigh. Barnabas introduced him <hi type="italic">to the apostles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.27">Acts ix. 27</reference>), and there were others <hi type="italic">that led him by the hand to Damascus</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.8">v. 8</reference>), but it was Christ that introduced and led him by the hand into this grace. <hi type="italic">By whom we have access by faith.</hi> By Christ as the author and principal agent, by faith as the means of this access. Not by Christ in consideration of any merit or desert of ours, but in consideration of our believing dependence upon him and resignation of ourselves to him. 2. Their happy standing in this state: <hi type="italic">wherein we stand.</hi> Not only wherein we are, but wherein we stand, a posture that denotes our discharge from guilt; <hi type="italic">we stand in the judgment</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.5">Ps. i. 5</reference>), not cast, as convicted criminals, but our dignity and honour secured, not thrown to the ground, as abjects. The phrase denotes also our progress; while we stand, we are going. We must not lie down, as if we had already attained, but stand as those that are pressing forward, stand as servants attending on Christ our master. The phrase denotes, further, our perseverance: we stand firmly and safely, upheld by the power of God; stand as soldiers stand, that keep their ground, not borne down by the power of the enemy. It denotes not only our admission to, but our confirmation in, the favour of God. It is not in the court of heaven as in earthly courts, where high places are slippery places: but we stand in a humble confidence of this very thing <hi type="italic">that he who has begun the good work will perform it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.6">Phil. i. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen30553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30554" type="x-p"/> III. <hi type="italic">We rejoice in hope of the glory of God.</hi> Besides the happiness in hand, there is a happiness in hope, <hi type="italic">the glory of God,</hi> the glory which God will put upon the saints in heaven, glory which will consist in the vision and fruition of God. 1. Those, and those only, that have access by faith into the grace of God now may hope for the glory of God hereafter. There is no good hope of glory but what is founded in grace; grace is glory begun, the earnest and assurance of glory. <hi type="italic">He will give grace and glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.84.11">Ps. lxxxiv. 11</reference>. 2. Those who hope for the glory of God hereafter have enough to rejoice in now. It is the duty of those that hope for heaven to rejoice in that hope. <div eID="gen30554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30555" type="x-p"/> IV. <hi type="italic">We glory in tribulations also;</hi> not only notwithstanding our tribulations (these do not hinder our rejoicing in hope of the glory of God), but even in our tribulations, as they are working for us the weight of glory, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.17">2 Cor. iv. 17</reference>. Observe, What a growing increasing happiness the happiness of the saints is: <hi type="italic">Not only so.</hi> One would think such peace, such grace, such glory, and such a joy in hope of it, were more than such poor undeserving creatures as we are could pretend to; and yet it is <hi type="italic">not only so:</hi> there are more instances of our happiness—<hi type="italic">we glory in tribulations also,</hi> especially tribulations for righteousness' sake, which seemed the greatest objection against the saints' happiness, whereas really their happiness did not only consist with, but take rise from, those tribulations. <hi type="italic">They rejoiced that they were counted worthy to suffer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.5.41">Acts v. 41</reference>. This being the hardest point, he sets himself to show the grounds and reasons of it. How come we to glory in tribulations? Why, because tribulations, by a chain of causes, greatly befriend hope, which he shows in the method of its influence. 1. <hi type="italic">Tribulation worketh patience,</hi> not in and of itself, but the powerful grace of God working in and with the tribulation. It proves, and by proving improves, patience, as parts and gifts increase by exercise. It is not the efficient cause, but yields the occasion, as steel is hardened by the fire. See how God brings meat out of the eater, and sweetness out of the strong. That which worketh patience is matter of joy; for patience does us more good than tribulations can do us hurt. Tribulation in itself worketh impatience; but, as it is sanctified to the saints, it worketh patience. 2. <hi type="italic">Patience experience,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.4">v. 4</reference>. It works an experience of God, and the songs he gives in the night; the patient sufferers have the greatest experience of the divine consolations, which abound as afflictions abound. It works an experience of ourselves. It is by tribulation that we make an experiment of our own sincerity, and therefore such tribulations are called trials. It works, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dokimen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">an approbation,</hi> as he is approved that has passed the test. Thus Job's tribulation wrought patience, and that patience produced an approbation, that still he <hi type="italic">holds fast his integrity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.2.3">Job ii. 3</reference>. 3. <hi type="italic">Experience hope.</hi> He who, being thus tried, comes forth as gold, will thereby be encouraged to hope. This experiment, or approbation, is not so much the ground, as the evidence, of our hope, and a special friend to it. Experience of God is a prop to our hope; he that hath delivered doth and will. Experience of ourselves helps to evidence our sincerity. 4. This <hi type="italic">hope maketh not ashamed;</hi> that is, it is a hope that will not deceive us. Nothing confounds more than disappointment. Everlasting shame and confusion will be caused by the perishing of the expectation of the wicked, <hi type="italic">but the hope of the righteous shall be gladness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.28">Prov. x. 28</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Ps.22.5">Ps. xxii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.71.1">lxxi. 1</reference>. Or, It maketh not ashamed of our sufferings. Though <hi type="italic">we are counted as the offscouring of all things, and trodden under foot as the mire in the streets,</hi> yet, having hopes of glory, we are not ashamed of these sufferings. It is in a good cause, for a good Master, and in good hope; and therefore we are not ashamed. We will never think ourselves disparaged by sufferings that are likely to end so well. <hi type="italic">Because the love of God is shed abroad.</hi> This hope will not disappoint us, because it is sealed with the Holy Spirit as a Spirit of love. It is the gracious work of the blessed Spirit to shed abroad the love of God in the hearts of all the saints. <hi type="italic">The love of God,</hi> that is, the sense of God's love to us, drawing out love in us to him again. Or, The great effects of his love: (1.) Special grace; and, (2.) The pleasant gust or sense of it. <hi type="italic">It is shed abroad,</hi> as sweet ointment, perfuming the soul, as rain watering it and making it fruitful. The ground of all our comfort and holiness, and perseverance in both, is laid in the <hi type="italic">shedding abroad of the love of God in our hearts;</hi> it is this which constrains us, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.14">2 Cor. v. 14</reference>. Thus are we drawn and held by the bonds of love. Sense of God's love to us will make us not ashamed, either of our hope in him or our sufferings for him.
entries.c82eda15c78b7a1645d90a284a056098557d5660: <div eID="gen30555" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The First and the Second Adam; The Influence of Grace. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 58.)</title> <div sID="gen30556" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly. <hi type="super">7</hi> For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die. <hi type="super">8</hi> But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. <hi type="super">9</hi> Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him. <hi type="super">10</hi> For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life. <hi type="super">11</hi> And not only <hi type="italic">so,</hi> but we also joy in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom we have now received the atonement. <hi type="super">12</hi> Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned: 13 (For until the law sin was in the world: but sin is not imputed when there is no law. <hi type="super">14</hi> Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam's transgression, who is the figure of him that was to come. <hi type="super">15</hi> But not as the offence, so also <hi type="italic">is</hi> the free gift. For if through the offence of one many be dead, much more the grace of God, and the gift by grace, <hi type="italic">which is</hi> by one man, Jesus Christ, hath abounded unto many. <hi type="super">16</hi> And not as <hi type="italic">it was</hi> by one that sinned, <hi type="italic">so is</hi> the gift: for the judgment <hi type="italic">was</hi> by one to condemnation, but the free gift <hi type="italic">is</hi> of many offences unto justification. <hi type="super">17</hi> For if by one man's offence death reigned by one; much more they which receive abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life by one, Jesus Christ.) <hi type="super">18</hi> Therefore as by the offence of one <hi type="italic">judgment came</hi> upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one <hi type="italic">the free gift came</hi> upon all men unto justification of life. <hi type="super">19</hi> For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. <hi type="super">20</hi> Moreover the law entered, that the offence might abound. But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound: <hi type="super">21</hi> That as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord. <div eID="gen30556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30557" type="x-p"/> The apostle here describes the fountain and foundation of justification, laid in the death of the Lord Jesus. The streams are very sweet, but, if you run them up to the spring-head, you will find it to be Christ's dying for us; it is in the precious stream of Christ's blood that all these privileges come flowing to us: and therefore he enlarges upon this instance of the love of God which is shed abroad. Three things he takes notice of for the explication and illustration of this doctrine:—1. The persons he died for, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.6-Rom.5.8">v. 6-8</reference>. 2. The precious fruits of his death, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.9-Rom.5.11">v. 9-11</reference>. 3. The parallel he runs between the communication of sin and death by the first Adam and of righteousness and life by the second Adam, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.12-Rom.5.21">v. 12, to the end</reference>. <div eID="gen30557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30558" type="x-p"/> I. The character we were under when Christ died for us. <div eID="gen30558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30559" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">We were without strength</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.6">v. 6</reference>), in a sad condition; and, which is worse, altogether unable to help ourselves out of that condition—lost, and no visible way open for our recovery—our condition deplorable, and in a manner desperate; and, therefore our salvation is here said to come <hi type="italic">in due time.</hi> God's time to help and save is when those that are to be saved are without strength, that his own power and grace may be the more magnified, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">Deut. xxxii. 36</reference>. It is the manner of God to help at a dead lift, <div eID="gen30559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30560" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">He died for the ungodly;</hi> not only helpless creatures, and therefore likely to perish, but guilty sinful creatures, and therefore deserving to perish; not only mean and worthless, but vile and obnoxious, unworthy of such favour with the holy God. Being ungodly, they had need of one to die for them, to satisfy for guilt, and to bring in a righteousness. This he illustrates (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.7-Rom.5.8">v. 7, 8</reference>) as an unparalleled instance of love; herein God's thoughts and ways were above ours. Compare <reference osisRef="John.15.13-John.15.14">John xv. 13, 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">Greater love has no man.</hi> (1.) One would hardly <hi type="italic">die for a righteous man,</hi> that is, an innocent man, one that is unjustly condemned; every body will pity such a one, but few will put such a value upon his life as either to hazard, or much less to deposit, their own in his stead. (2.) It may be, one might perhaps be persuaded <hi type="italic">to die for a good man,</hi> that is, a useful man, who is more than barely a righteous man. Many that are good themselves yet do but little good to others; but those that are useful commonly get themselves well beloved, and meet with some that in a case of necessity would venture to be their <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">antipsychoi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">would engage life for life,</hi> would be their bail, body for body. Paul was, in this sense, a very good man, one that was very useful, and he met with some that for his life laid down their own necks, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.4">ch. xvi. 4</reference>. And yet observe how he qualifies this: it is but some that would do so, and it is a daring act if they do it, it must be some bold venturing soul; and, after all, it is but a <hi type="italic">peradventure.</hi> (3.) <hi type="italic">But Christ died for sinners</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.8">v. 8</reference>), neither righteous nor good; not only such as were useless, but such as were guilty and obnoxious; not only such as there would be no loss of should they perish, but such whose destruction would greatly redound to the glory of God's justice, being malefactors and criminals that ought to die. Some think he alludes to a common distinction the Jews had of their people into <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ndyqym</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">righteous,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hsdym</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">merciful</hi> (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1">Isa. xvii. 1</reference>), and <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">rssym</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">wicked.</hi> Now herein <hi type="italic">God commended his love,</hi> not only proved or evidenced his love (he might have done that at a cheaper rate), but magnified it and made it illustrious. This circumstance did greatly magnify and advance his love, not only put it past dispute, but rendered it the object of the greatest wonder and admiration: "Now my creatures shall see that I love them, I will give them such an instance of it as shall be without parallel." <hi type="italic">Commendeth his love,</hi> as merchants commend their goods when they would put them off. This commending of his love was in order to the shedding abroad of his love in our hearts by the Holy Ghost. He evinces his love in the most winning, affecting, endearing way imaginable. <hi type="italic">While we were yet sinners,</hi> implying that we were not to be always sinners, there should be a change wrought; for he died to save us, not in our sins, but from our sins; but we were yet sinners when he died for us. (4.) Nay, which is more, <hi type="italic">we were enemies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.10">v. 10</reference>), not only malefactors, but traitors and rebels, in arms against the government; the worst kind of malefactors and of all malefactors the most obnoxious. The carnal mind is not only an enemy to God, but enmity itself, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.7">ch. viii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.21">Col. i. 21</reference>. This enmity is a mutual enmity, God loathing the sinner, and the sinner loathing God, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.8">Zech. xi. 8</reference>. And that for such as these Christ should die is such a mystery, such a paradox, such an unprecedented instance of love, that it may well be our business to eternity to adore and wonder at it. This is a commendation of love indeed. Justly might he who had thus loved us make it one of the laws of his kingdom that we should love our enemies. <div eID="gen30560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30561" type="x-p"/> II. The precious fruits of his death. <div eID="gen30561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30562" type="x-p"/> 1. Justification and reconciliation are the first and primary fruit of the death of Christ: <hi type="italic">We are justified by his blood</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">reconciled by his death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.10">v. 10</reference>. Sin is pardoned, the sinner accepted as righteous, the quarrel taken up, the enmity slain, an end made of iniquity, and an everlasting righteousness brought in. This is done, that is, Christ has done all that was requisite on his part to be done in order hereunto, and, immediately upon our believing, we are actually put into a state of justification and reconciliation. <hi type="italic">Justified by his blood.</hi> Our justification is ascribed to the blood of Christ because <hi type="italic">without blood there is no remission</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.22">Heb. ix. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">The blood is the life,</hi> and that must go to make atonement. In all the propitiatory sacrifices, the sprinkling of the blood was of the essence of the sacrifice. It was <hi type="italic">the blood that made an atonement for the soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.17.11">Lev. xvii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen30562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30563" type="x-p"/> 2. Hence results salvation from wrath: <hi type="italic">Saved from wrath</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">saved by his life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.10">v. 10</reference>. When that which hinders our salvation is taken away, the salvation must needs follow. Nay, the argument holds very strongly; if God justified and reconciled us when we were enemies, and put himself to so much charge to do it, much more will he save us when we are justified and reconciled. He that has done the greater, which is of enemies to make us friends, will certainly the less, which is when we are friends to use us friendly and to be kind to us. And therefore the apostle, once and again, speaks of it with a <hi type="italic">much more.</hi> He that hath digged so deep to lay the foundation will no doubt build upon that foundation.—<hi type="italic">We shall be saved from wrath,</hi> from hell and damnation. It is the wrath of God that is the fire of hell; <hi type="italic">the wrath to come,</hi> so it is called, <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.10">1 Thess. i. 10</reference>. The final justification and absolution of believers at the great day, together with the fitting and preparing of them for it, are the salvation from wrath here spoken of; it is the perfecting of the work of grace.—<hi type="italic">Reconciled by his death, saved by his life.</hi> His life here spoken of is not to be understood of his life in the flesh, but his life in heaven, that life which ensued after his death. Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.14.9">ch. xiv. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">He was dead, and is alive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.18">Rev. i. 18</reference>. We are reconciled by Christ humbled, we are saved by Christ exalted. The dying Jesus laid the foundation, in satisfying for sin, and slaying the enmity, and so making us salvable; thus is the partition-wall broken down, atonement made, and the attainder reversed; but it is the living Jesus that perfects the work: <hi type="italic">he lives to make intercession,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.7.25">Heb. vii. 25</reference>. It is Christ, in his exaltation, that by his word and Spirit effectually calls, and changes, and reconciles us to God, is our Advocate with the Father, and so completes and consummates our salvation. Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.4.25">ch. iv. 25</reference> and <reference osisRef="Rom.8.34">viii. 34</reference>. Christ dying was the testator, who bequeathed us the legacy; but Christ living is the executor, who pays it. Now the arguing is very strong. He that puts himself to the charge of purchasing our salvation will not decline the trouble of applying it. <div eID="gen30563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30564" type="x-p"/> 3. All this produces, as a further privilege, our <hi type="italic">joy in God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.11">v. 11</reference>. God is now so far from being a terror to us that he is our <hi type="italic">joy, and our hope in the day of evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.17.17">Jer. xvii. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">We are reconciled and saved from wrath.</hi> Iniquity, blessed be God, <hi type="italic">shall not be our ruin. And not only so,</hi> there is more in it yet, a constant stream of favours; we not only go to heaven, but go to heaven triumphantly; not only get into the harbour, but come in with full sail: <hi type="italic">We joy in God,</hi> not only saved from his wrath, but solacing ourselves in his love, and this through Jesus Christ, who is the Alpha and the Omega, the foundation-stone and the top-stone of all our comforts and hopes—not only <hi type="italic">our salvation, but our strength and our song;</hi> and all this (which he repeats as a string he loved to be harping upon) by virtue of the atonement, for by him we Christians, we believers, have now, now in gospel times, or now in this life, <hi type="italic">received the atonement,</hi> which was typified by the sacrifices under the law, and is an earnest of our happiness in heaven. True believers do by Jesus Christ receive the atonement. Receiving the atonement is our actual reconciliation to God in justification, grounded upon Christ's satisfaction. To <hi type="italic">receive the atonement</hi> is, (1.) To give our consent to the atonement, approving of, and agreeing to, those methods which Infinite Wisdom has taken of saving a guilty world by the blood of a crucified Jesus, being willing and glad to be saved in a gospel way and upon gospel terms. (2.) To take the comfort of the atonement, which is the fountain and the foundation of our joy in God. Now <hi type="italic">we joy in God,</hi> now we do indeed <hi type="italic">receive the atonement,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kauchomenoi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">glorying</hi> in it. God hath received the atonement (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Matt. iii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.17.5">xvii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.2">xxviii. 2</reference>): if we but receive it, the work is done. <div eID="gen30564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30565" type="x-p"/> III. The parallel that the apostle runs between the communication of sin and death by the first Adam and of righteousness and life by the second Adam ( <reference osisRef="Rom.5.12-Rom.5.21">v. 12, to the end</reference>), which not only illustrates the truth he is discoursing of, but tends very much to the commending of the love of God and the comforting of the hearts of true believers, in showing a correspondence between our fall and our recovery, and not only a like, but a much greater power in the second Adam to make us happy, than there was in the first to make us miserable. Now, for the opening of this, observe, <div eID="gen30565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30566" type="x-p"/> 1. A general truth laid down as the foundation of his discourse—that Adam was a type of Christ (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who is the figure of him that was to come.</hi> Christ is therefore called the <hi type="italic">last Adam,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.45">1 Cor. xv. 45</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.5.22">v. 22</reference>. In this Adam was a type of Christ, that in the covenant-transactions that were between God and him, and in the consequent events of those transactions, Adam was a public person. God dealt with Adam and Adam acted as such a one, as a common father and factor, root and representative, of and for all his posterity; so that what he did in that station, as agent for us, we may be said to have done in him, and what was done to him may be said to have been done to us in him. Thus Jesus Christ, the Mediator, acted as a public person, the head of all the elect, dealt with God for them, as their father, factor, root, and representative—died for them, rose for them, entered within the veil for them, did all for them. When Adam failed, we failed with him; when Christ performed, he performed for us. Thus was Adam <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">typos tou mellontos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the figure of him that was to come,</hi> to come to repair that breach which Adam had made. <div eID="gen30566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30567" type="x-p"/> 2. A more particular explication of the parallel, in which observe, <div eID="gen30567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30568" type="x-p"/> (1.) How Adam, as a public person, communicated sin and death to all his posterity (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">By one man sin entered.</hi> We see the world under a deluge of sin and death, full of iniquities and full of calamities. Now, it is worth while to enquire what is the spring that feeds it, and you will find it to be the general corruption of nature; and at what gap it entered, and you will find it to have been Adam's first sin. It was <hi type="italic">by one man,</hi> and he the first man (for if any had been before him they would have been free), that one man from whom, as from the root, we all spring. [1.] By him <hi type="italic">sin entered.</hi> When God pronounced all very good (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.31">Gen. i. 31</reference>) there was no sin in the world; it was when Adam ate forbidden fruit that sin made its entry. Sin had before entered into the world of angels, when many of them revolted from their allegiance and left their first estate; but it never entered into the world of mankind till Adam sinned. Then it entered as an enemy, to kill and destroy, as a thief, to rob and despoil; and a dismal entry it was. Then entered the guilt of Adam's sin imputed to posterity, and a general corruption and depravedness of nature. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Eph ho</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">for that</hi> (so we read it), rather <hi type="italic">in whom, all have sinned.</hi> Sin entered into the world by Adam, for in him we all sinned. As, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.22">1 Cor. xv. 22</reference>, <hi type="italic">in Adam all die;</hi> so here, <hi type="italic">in him all have sinned;</hi> for it is agreeable to the law of all nations that the acts of a public person be accounted theirs whom they represent; and what a whole body does every member of the same body may be said to do. Now Adam acted thus as a public person, by the sovereign ordination and appointment of God, and yet that founded upon a natural necessity; for God, as the author of nature, had made this the law of nature, that man should beget in his own likeness, and so the other creatures. In Adam therefore, as in a common receptacle, the whole nature of man was reposited, from him to flow down in a channel to his posterity; for all mankind are made <hi type="italic">of one blood</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.26">Acts xvii. 26</reference>), so that according as this nature proves through his standing or falling, before he puts it out of his hands, accordingly it is propagated from him. Adam therefore sinning and falling, the nature became guilty and corrupt, and is so derived. Thus in him all have sinned. [2.] <hi type="italic">Death by sin,</hi> for death is the wages of sin. Sin, when it is finished, brings forth death. When sin came, of course death came with it. Death is here put for all that misery which is the due desert of sin, temporal, spiritual, eternal death. If Adam had not sinned, he had not died; the threatening was, <hi type="italic">In the day thou eatest thou shall surely die,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.2.17">Gen. ii. 17</reference>. [3.] <hi type="italic">So death passed,</hi> that is, a sentence of death was passed, as upon a criminal, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dielthen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">passed through</hi> all men, as an infectious disease passes through a town, so that none escape it. It is the universal fate, without exception: death passes upon all. There are common calamities incident to human life which do abundantly prove this. <hi type="italic">Death reigned,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.14">v. 14</reference>. He speaks of death as a mighty prince, and his monarchy the most absolute, universal, and lasting monarchy. None are exempted from its sceptre; it is a monarchy that will survive all other earthly rule, authority, and power, for it is the last enemy, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.26">1 Cor. xv. 26</reference>. Those sons of Belial that will be subject to no other rule cannot avoid being subject to this. Now all this we may thank Adam for; from him sin and death descend. Well may we say, as that good man, observing the change that a fit of sickness had made in his countenance, <hi type="italic">O Adam!</hi> what hast thou done? <div eID="gen30568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30569" type="x-p"/> Further, to clear this, he shows that sin did not commence with the law of Moses, but was <hi type="italic">in the world until,</hi> or <hi type="italic">before,</hi> that law; therefore that law of Moses is not the only rule of life, for there was a rule, and that rule was transgressed, before the law was given. It likewise intimates that we cannot be justified by our obedience to the law of Moses, any more than we were condemned by and for our disobedience to it. Sin was in the world before the law; witness Cain's murder, the apostasy of the old world, the wickedness of Sodom. His inference hence is, Therefore there was a law; for <hi type="italic">sin is not imputed where there is no law.</hi> Original sin is a want of conformity to, and actual sin is a transgression of, the law of God: therefore all were under some law. His proof of it is, <hi type="italic">Death reigned from Adam to Moses,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.14">v. 14</reference>. It is certain that death could not have reigned if sin had not set up the throne for him. This proves that sin was in the world before the law, and original sin, for death reigned over those that had not sinned any actual sin, that <hi type="italic">had not sinned after the similitude of Adam's transgression,</hi> never sinned in their own persons as Adam did—which is to be understood of infants, that were never guilty of actual sin, and yet died, because Adam's sin was imputed to them. This reign of death seems especially to refer to those violent and extraordinary judgments which were long before Moses, as the deluge and the destruction of Sodom, which involved infants. It is a great proof of original sin that little children, who were never guilty of any actual transgression, are yet liable to very terrible diseases, casualties, and deaths, which could by no means be reconciled with the justice and righteousness of God if they were not chargeable with guilt. <div eID="gen30569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30570" type="x-p"/> (2.) How, in correspondence to this, Christ, as a public person, communicates righteousness and life to all true believers, who are his spiritual seed. And in this he shows not only wherein the resemblance holds, but, <hi type="italic">ex abundanti,</hi> wherein the communication of grace and love by Christ <hi type="italic">goes beyond</hi> the communication of guilt and wrath by Adam. Observe, <div eID="gen30570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30571" type="x-p"/> [1.] Wherein the resemblance holds. This is laid down most fully, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.18-Rom.5.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. <div eID="gen30571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30572" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First, By the offence and disobedience of one many were made sinners, and judgment came upon all men to condemnation.</hi> Here observe, 1. That Adam's sin was disobedience, disobedience to a plain and express command: and it was a command of trial. The thing he did was therefore evil because it was forbidden, and not otherwise; but this opened the door to other sins, though itself seemingly small. 2. That the malignity and poison of sin are very strong and spreading, else the guilt of Adam's sin would not have reached so far, nor have been so deep and long a stream. Who would think there should be so much evil in sin? 3. That by Adam's sin many are made sinners: <hi type="italic">many,</hi> that is, all his posterity; said to be many, in opposition to the one that offended, <hi type="italic">Made sinners,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">katestathesan.</hi></hi> It denotes the making of us such by a judicial act: we were cast as sinners by due course of law. 4. That judgment is come to condemnation upon all those that by Adam's disobedience were made sinners. Being convicted, we are condemned. All the race of mankind lie under a sentence, like an attainder upon a family. There is judgment given and recorded against us in the court of heaven; and, if the judgment be not reversed, we are likely to sink under it to eternity. <div eID="gen30572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30573" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> In like manner, <hi type="italic">by the righteousness and obedience of one</hi> (and that one is Jesus Christ, the second Adam), <hi type="italic">are many made righteous,</hi> and so the <hi type="italic">free gift comes upon all.</hi> It is observable how the apostle inculcates this truth, and repeats it again and again, as a truth of very great consequence. Here observe, 1. The nature of Christ's righteousness, how it is brought in; it is by his obedience. The disobedience of the first Adam ruined us, the obedience of the second Adam saves us,—his obedience to the law of mediation, which was that he should fulfil all righteousness, and then make his soul an offering for sin. By his obedience to this law he wrought out a righteousness for us, satisfied God's justice, and so made way for us into his favour. 2. The fruit of it. (1.) There is a <hi type="italic">free gift come upon all men,</hi> that is, it is made and offered promiscuously to all. The salvation wrought is a <hi type="italic">common salvation;</hi> the proposals are general, the tender free; whoever will may come, and take of these waters of life. This free gift is to all believers, upon their believing, <hi type="italic">unto justification of life.</hi> It is not only a justification that frees from death, but that entitles to life. (2.) <hi type="italic">Many shall be made righteous</hi>—many compared with one, or as many as belong to the election of grace, which, though but a few as they are scattered up and down in the world, yet will be a great many when they come all together. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Katastathesontai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">they shall be constituted</hi> righteous, as by letters patent. Now the antithesis between these two, our ruin by Adam and our recovery by Christ, is obvious enough. <div eID="gen30573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30574" type="x-p"/> [2.] Wherein the communication of grace and love by Christ goes beyond the communication of guilt and wrath by Adam; and this he shows, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.15-Rom.5.17">v. 15-17</reference>. It is designed for the magnifying of the riches of Christ's love, and for the comfort and encouragement of believers, who, considering what a wound Adam's sin has made, might begin to despair of a proportionable remedy. His expressions are a little intricate, but this he seems to intend:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> If guilt and wrath be communicated, much more shall grace and love; for it is agreeable to the idea we have of the divine goodness to suppose that he should be more ready to save upon an imputed righteousness than to condemn upon an imputed guilt: <hi type="italic">Much more the grace of God, and the gift by grace.</hi> God's goodness is, of all his attributes, in a special manner his glory, and it is that grace that is the root (his favour to us in Christ), and the gift is by grace. We know that God is rather inclined to show mercy; punishing is his strange work. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> If there was so much power and efficacy, as it seems there was, in the sin of a man, who was of the earth, earthy, to condemn us, much more are there power and efficacy in the righteousness and grace of Christ, who is the Lord from heaven, to justify and save us. The <hi type="italic">one man</hi> that saves us is Jesus Christ. Surely Adam could not propagate so strong a poison but Jesus Christ could propagate as strong an antidote, and much stronger. 3. It is but the guilt of one single offence of Adam's that is laid to our charge: <hi type="italic">The judgment was</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ex henos eis katakrima,</hi></hi> <hi type="italic">by one,</hi> that is, by one offence, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.16-Rom.5.17">v. 16, 17</reference>, <hi type="italic">Margin.</hi> But from Jesus Christ we receive and derive an <hi type="italic">abundance of grace, and of the gift of righteousness.</hi> The stream of grace and righteousness is deeper and broader than the stream of guilt; for this righteousness does not only take away the guilt of that one offence, but of many other offences, even of all. God in Christ forgives all trespasses, <reference osisRef="Col.2.13">Col. ii. 13</reference>. 4. By Adam's sin <hi type="italic">death reigned;</hi> but by Christ's righteousness there is not only a period put to the reign of death, but believers are preferred to <hi type="italic">reign of life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.17">v. 17</reference>. In and by the righteousness of Christ we have not only a charter of pardon, but a patent of honour, are not only freed from our chains, but, like Joseph, advanced to the second chariot, and made unto our God kings and priests—not only pardoned, but preferred. See this observed, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5-Rev.1.6">Rev. i. 5, 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.9-Rev.5.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. We are by Christ and his righteousness entitled to, and instated in, more and greater privileges than we lost by the offence of Adam. The plaster is wider than the wound, and more healing than the wound is killing. <div eID="gen30574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30575" type="x-p"/> IV. In the <reference osisRef="Rom.5.20-Rom.5.21">last two verses</reference> the apostle seems to anticipate an objection which is expressed, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.19">Gal. iii. 19</reference>, <hi type="italic">Wherefore then serveth the law?</hi> Answer, 1. <hi type="italic">The law entered that the offence might abound.</hi> Not to make sin to abound the more in itself, otherwise than as sin takes occasion by the commandment, but to discover the abounding sinfulness of it. The glass discovers the spots, but does not cause them. When the commandment came into the world sin revived, as the letting of a clearer light into a room discovers the dust and filth which were there before, but were not seen. It was like the searching of a wound, which is necessary to the cure. <hi type="italic">The offence,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">to paraptoma</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">that offence,</hi> the sin of Adam, the extending of the guilt of it to us, and the effect of the corruption in us, are the abounding of that offence which appeared upon the entry of the law. 2. <hi type="italic">That grace might much more abound</hi>—that the terrors of the law might make gospel-comforts so much the sweeter. Sin abounded among the Jews; and, to those of them that were converted to the faith of Christ, did not grace much more abound in the remitting of so much guilt and the subduing of so much corruption? The greater the strength of the enemy, the greater the honour of the conqueror. This abounding of grace he illustrates, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.21">v. 21</reference>. As the reign of a tyrant and oppressor is a foil to set off the succeeding reign of a just and gentle prince and to make it the more illustrious, so doth the reign of sin set off the reign of grace. <hi type="italic">Sin reigned unto death;</hi> it was a cruel bloody reign. But <hi type="italic">grace reigns</hi> to life, <hi type="italic">eternal life,</hi> and this <hi type="italic">through righteousness,</hi> righteousness imputed to us for justification, implanted in us for sanctification; and both by <hi type="italic">Jesus Christ our Lord,</hi> through the power and efficacy of Christ, the great prophet, priest, and king, of his church.  <chapter eID="Rom.5"/> <div eID="gen30575" type="x-p"/>

entries.fc542373eb915c9f1fb53b38d66ec04fcd2ce3c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16432"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Rom.5.1-Rom.5.11">Ro 5:1-11</reference>. The Blessed Effects of Justification by Faith.</title> <div sID="gen31895" type="x-p"/> The proof of this doctrine being now concluded, the apostle comes here to treat of its fruits, reserving the full consideration of this topic to another stage of the argument (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.1-Rom.8.39">Ro 8:1-39</reference>).<div eID="gen31895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31896" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16432"/><hi type="bold">1. Therefore being--</hi>"having been."<div eID="gen31896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">justified by faith, we have peace with God, &c.--</hi>If we are to be guided by manuscript authority, the true reading here, beyond doubt, is, "Let us have peace"; a reading, however, which most reject, because they think it unnatural to exhort men to have what it belongs to God to give, because the apostle is not here giving exhortations, but stating matters of fact. But as it seems hazardous to set aside the decisive testimony of manuscripts, as to what the apostle did write, in favor of what we merely think he ought to have written, let us pause and ask--If it be the privilege of the justified to "have peace with God," why might not the apostle begin his enumeration of the fruits of justification by calling on believers to "realize" this peace as belonged to them, or cherish the joyful consciousness of it as their own? And if this is what he has done, it would not be necessary to continue in the same style, and the other fruits of justification might be set down, simply as matters of fact. This "peace" is first a change in God's relation to us; and next, as the consequence of this, a change on our part towards Him. God, on the one hand, has "reconciled us to Himself by Jesus Christ" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.18">2Co 5:18</reference>); and we, on the other hand, setting our seal to this, "are reconciled to God" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.20">2Co 5:20</reference>). The "propitiation" is the meeting-place; there the controversy on both sides terminates in an honorable and eternal "peace." <div eID="gen31897" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ee4ca98a440e9ea8bc4c50a547882d54450dfe4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16433"/><div sID="gen31898" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16433"/><hi type="bold">2. By whom also we have--</hi>"have had"<div eID="gen31898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">access by faith into this grace--</hi>favor with God.<div eID="gen31899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wherein we stand--</hi>that is "To that same faith which first gave us 'peace with God' we owe our introduction into that permanent standing in the favor of God which the justified enjoy." As it is difficult to distinguish this from the peace first mentioned, we regard it as merely an additional phase of the same [Meyer, Philippi, Mehring], rather than something new [Beza, Tholuck, Hodge].<div eID="gen31900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and rejoice--</hi>"glory," "boast," "triumph"--"rejoice" is not strong enough.<div eID="gen31901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31902" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in hope of the glory of God--</hi>On "hope," see on <reference osisRef="Rom.5.4">Ro 5:4</reference>. <div eID="gen31902" type="x-p"/>
entries.2359793de01a4d31969bdbc971fa3f0cca31a782: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16434"/><div sID="gen31903" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16434"/><hi type="bold">3-4. we glory in tribulation also; knowing that tribulation worketh patience--</hi>Patience is the quiet endurance of what we cannot but wish removed, whether it be the withholding of promised good (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.25">Ro 8:25</reference>), or the continued experience of positive ill (as here). There is indeed a patience of unrenewed nature, which has something noble in it, though in many cases the offspring of pride, if not of something lower. Men have been known to endure every form of privation, torture, and death, without a murmur and without even visible emotion, merely because they deemed it unworthy of them to sink under unavoidable ill. But this proud, stoical hardihood has nothing in common with the grace of patience--which is either the meek endurance of ill because it is of God (<reference osisRef="Job.1.21">Job 1:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.22">22</reference>; 2:10), or the calm waiting for promised good till His time to dispense it come (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.36">He 10:36</reference>); in the full persuasion that such trials are divinely appointed, are the needed discipline of God's children, are but for a definite period, and are not sent without abundant promises of "songs in the night." If such be the "patience" which "tribulation worketh," no wonder that <div eID="gen31903" type="x-p"/>
entries.810fb9dacb2a28a0cb381596cb2e375c535f493d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16436"/><div sID="gen31907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16436"/><hi type="bold">5. And hope maketh not ashamed--</hi>putteth not to shame, as empty hopes do.<div eID="gen31907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because the love of God--</hi>that is, not "our love to God," as the Romish and some Protestant expositors (following some of the Fathers) represent it; but clearly "God's love to us"--as most expositors agree.<div eID="gen31908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is shed abroad--</hi>literally, "poured forth," that is, copiously diffused (compare <reference osisRef="John.7.38">Joh 7:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.6">Tit 3:6</reference>).<div eID="gen31909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the Holy Ghost which is--</hi>rather, "was."<div eID="gen31910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">given unto us--</hi>that is, at the great Pentecostal effusion, which is viewed as the formal donation of the Spirit to the Church of God, for all time and for each believer. (The Holy Ghost is here first introduced in this Epistle.) It is as if the apostle had said, "And how can this hope of glory, which as believers we cherish, put us to shame, when we feel God Himself, by His Spirit given to us, drenching our hearts in sweet, all-subduing sensations of His wondrous love to us in Christ Jesus?" This leads the apostle to expatiate on the amazing character of that love. <div eID="gen31911" type="x-p"/>
entries.906fc4d29cff7e09b88cfe99172ff2f4b8ec616a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16437"/><div sID="gen31912" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16437"/><hi type="bold">6-8. For when we were yet without strength--</hi>that is, powerless to deliver ourselves, and so ready to perish.<div eID="gen31912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in due time--</hi>at the appointed season.<div eID="gen31913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31914" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Christ died for the ungodly--</hi>Three signal properties of God's love are here given: First, "Christ died for the ungodly," whose character, so far from meriting any interposition in their behalf, was altogether repulsive to the eye of God; second, He did this "when they were without strength"--with nothing between them and perdition but that self-originating divine compassion; third, He did this "at the due time," when it was most fitting that it should take place (compare <reference osisRef="Gal.4.4">Ga 4:4</reference>), The two former of these properties the apostle now proceeds to illustrate. <div eID="gen31914" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fde61c65591797816b3728922ccfd6bab0f8a22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16440"/><div sID="gen31924" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16440"/><hi type="bold">9-10. Much more then, being--</hi>"having been"<div eID="gen31924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31925" type="x-p"/> now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him. <div eID="gen31925" type="x-p"/>
entries.17ff319de5d6173ae7f3774bad6b09cc775e4990: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16442"/><div sID="gen31928" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16442"/><hi type="bold">11. And not only so, but we also joy--</hi>rather, "glory."<div eID="gen31928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31929" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, by--</hi>"through"<div eID="gen31929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31930" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whom we have now received the atonement--</hi>rather, "the reconciliation" (Margin), as the same word is rendered in <reference osisRef="Rom.5.10">Ro 5:10</reference> and in <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.18">2Co 5:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">19</reference>. (In fact, the earlier meaning of the English word "atonement" was "the reconciliation of two estranged parties") [Trench]. The foregoing effects of justification were all benefits to ourselves, calling for gratitude; this last may be termed a purely disinterested one. Our first feeling towards God, after we have found peace with Him, is that of clinging gratitude for so costly a salvation; but no sooner have we learned to cry, Abba, Father, under the sweet sense of reconciliation, than "gloriation" in Him takes the place of dread of Him, and now He appears to us "altogether lovely!"<div eID="gen31930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">On this section, Note, (1) How gloriously does the Gospel evince its divine origin by basing all acceptable obedience on "peace with God," laying the foundations of this peace in a righteous "justification" of the sinner "through our Lord Jesus Christ," and making this the entrance to a permanent standing in the divine favor, and a triumphant expectation of future glory! (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.1">Ro 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.2">2</reference>). Other peace, worthy of the name, there is none; and as those who are strangers to it rise not to the enjoyment of such high fellowship with God, so they have neither any taste for it nor desire after it. (2) As only believers possess the true secret of patience under trials, so, although "not joyous but grievous" in themselves (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.17">He 12:17</reference>), when trials divinely sent afford them the opportunity of evidencing their faith by the grace of patience under them, they should "count it all joy" (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.3">Ro 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.4">4</reference>; and see <reference osisRef="Jas.1.2">Jas 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.3">3</reference>). (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.3">3</reference>) "Hope," in the New Testament sense of the term, is not a lower degree of faith or assurance (as many now say, I hope for heaven, but am not sure of it); but invariably means "the confident expectation of future good." It presupposes faith; and what faith assures us will be ours, hope accordingly expects. In the nourishment of this hope, the soul's look outward to Christ for the ground of it, and inward upon ourselves for evidence of its reality, must act and react upon each other (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.2">Ro 5:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Rom.5.4">Ro 5:4</reference> compared). (4) It is the proper office of the Holy Ghost to beget in the soul the full conviction and joyful consciousness of the love of God in Christ Jesus to sinners of mankind, and to ourselves in particular; and where this exists, it carries with it such an assurance of final salvation as cannot deceive (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">Ro 5:5</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">5</reference>) The justification of sinful men is not in virtue of their amendment, but of "the blood of God's Son"; and while this is expressly affirmed in <reference osisRef="Rom.5.9">Ro 5:9</reference>, our reconciliation to God by the "death of His Son," affirmed in <reference osisRef="Rom.5.10">Ro 5:10</reference>, is but a variety of the same statement. In both, the blessing meant is the restoration of the sinner to a righteous standing in the sight of God; and in both, the meritorious ground of this, which is intended to be conveyed, is the expiatory sacrifice of God's Son. (6) Gratitude to God for redeeming love, if it could exist without delight in God Himself, would be a selfish and worthless feeling; but when the one rises into the other--</hi>the transporting sense of eternal "reconciliation" passing into "gloriation in God" Himself--then the lower is sanctified and sustained by the higher, and each feeling is perfective of the other (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.11">Ro 5:11</reference>).<div eID="gen31931" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Rom.5.12-Rom.5.21">Ro 5:12-21</reference>. Comparison and Contrast between Adam and Christ in Their Relation to the Human Family.</title> <div sID="gen31932" type="x-p"/> (This profound and most weighty section has occasioned an immense deal of critical and theological discussion, in which every point, and almost every clause, has been contested. We can here but set down what appears to us to be the only tenable view of it as a whole and of its successive clauses, with some slight indication of the grounds of our judgment). <div eID="gen31932" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7d54a6d1e4168cc02ae5b2b0830200d445f5395: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16443"/><div sID="gen31933" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16443"/><hi type="bold">12. Wherefore--</hi>that is, Things being so; referring back to the whole preceding argument.<div eID="gen31933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31934" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as by one man--</hi>Adam.<div eID="gen31934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sin--</hi>considered here in its guilt, criminality, penal desert.<div eID="gen31935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">entered into the world, and death by sin--</hi>as the penalty of sin.<div eID="gen31936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned--</hi>rather, "all sinned," that is, in that one man's first sin. Thus death reaches every individual of the human family, as the penalty due to himself. (So, in substance, Bengel, Hodge, Philippi). Here we should have expected the apostle to finish his sentence, in some such way as this: "Even so, by one man righteousness has entered into the world, and life by righteousness." But, instead of this, we have a digression, extending to five verses, to illustrate the important statement of <reference osisRef="Rom.5.12">Ro 5:12</reference>; and it is only at <reference osisRef="Rom.5.18">Ro 5:18</reference> that the comparison is resumed and finished. <div eID="gen31937" type="x-p"/>
entries.279e3f745cf522f8e104eec4335a03c79220efbe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16444"/><div sID="gen31938" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16444"/><hi type="bold">13-14. For until the law sin was in the world--</hi>that is during all the period from Adam "until the law" of Moses was given, God continued to treat men as sinners.<div eID="gen31938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31939" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but sin is not imputed where there is no law--</hi>"There must therefore have been a law during that period, because sin was then imputed"; as is now to be shown. <div eID="gen31939" type="x-p"/>
entries.526c578a3b04c5526efbb1231ce2020eb03b3c37: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16446"/><div sID="gen31943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16446"/><hi type="bold">15. But--</hi>"Yet," "Howbeit."<div eID="gen31943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31944" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not as the offence--</hi>"trespass."<div eID="gen31944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31945" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so also is the free gift--</hi>or "the gracious gift," "the gift of grace." The two cases present points of contrast as well as resemblance.<div eID="gen31945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">For if, &c.--</hi>rather, "For if through the offense of the one the many died (that is, in that one man's first sin), much more did the grace of God, and the free gift by grace, even that of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound unto the many." By "the many" is meant the mass of mankind represented respectively by Adam and Christ, as opposed, not to few, but to "the one" who represented them. By "the free gift" is meant (as in <reference osisRef="Rom.5.17">Ro 5:17</reference>) the glorious gift of justifying righteousness; this is expressly distinguished from "the grace of God," as the effect from the cause; and both are said to "abound" towards us in Christ--in what sense will appear in <reference osisRef="Rom.5.16">Ro 5:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.17">17</reference>. And the "much more," of the one case than the other, does not mean that we get much more of good by Christ than of evil by Adam (for it is not a case of quantity at all); but that we have much more reason to expect, or it is much more agreeable to our ideas of God, that the many should be benefited by the merit of one, than that they should suffer for the sin of one; and if the latter has happened, much more may we assure ourselves of the former [Philippi, Hodge]. <div eID="gen31946" type="x-p"/>
entries.743457ad326b709f3a4eff8910b22bea8d092750: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16447"/><div sID="gen31947" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16447"/><hi type="bold">16. And not as it was by one that sinned, so is the gift--</hi>"Another point of contrast may be mentioned."<div eID="gen31947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31948" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the judgment--</hi>"sentence."<div eID="gen31948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31949" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was by one--</hi>rather, "was of one," meaning not "one man," but, as appears from the next clause, "one offense."<div eID="gen31949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31950" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to condemnation, but the free gift--</hi>"gift of grace."<div eID="gen31950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31951" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is of many offences unto justification--</hi>a glorious point of contrast. "The condemnation by Adam was for one sin; but the justification by Christ is an absolution not only from the guilt of that first offense, mysteriously attaching to every individual of the race, but from the countless offenses it, to which, as a germ lodged in the bosom of every child of Adam, it unfolds itself in his life." This is the meaning of "grace abounding towards us in the abundance of the gift of righteousness." It is a grace not only rich in its character, but rich in detail; it is a "righteousness" not only rich in a complete justification of the guilty, condemned sinner; but rich in the amplitude of the ground which it covers, leaving no one sin of any of the justified uncancelled, but making him, though loaded with the guilt of myriads of offenses, "the righteousness of God in Christ." <div eID="gen31951" type="x-p"/>
entries.26f614ecf79244277529c0c700a92d591629423a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16448"/><div sID="gen31952" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16448"/><hi type="bold">17. For if by--</hi>"the"<div eID="gen31952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31953" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one man's offence death reigned by one--</hi>"through the one."<div eID="gen31953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31954" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">much more shall they which receive--</hi>"the"<div eID="gen31954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31955" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abundance of grace and of the gift of--</hi>justifying<div eID="gen31955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31956" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness ... reign in life by one Jesus Christ--</hi>"through the one." We have here the two ideas of <reference osisRef="Rom.5.15">Ro 5:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Rom.5.16">Ro 5:16</reference> sublimely combined into one, as if the subject had grown upon the apostle as he advanced in his comparison of the two cases. Here, for the first time in this section, he speaks of that LIFE which springs out of justification, in contrast with the death which springs from sin and follows condemnation. The proper idea of it therefore is, "Right to live"--"Righteous life"--life possessed and enjoyed with the good will, and in conformity with the eternal law, of "Him that sitteth on the Throne"; life therefore in its widest sense--life in the whole man and throughout the whole duration of human existence, the life of blissful and loving relationship to God in soul and body, for ever and ever. It is worthy of note, too, that while he says death "reigned over" us through Adam, he does not say Life "reigns over us" through Christ; lest he should seem to invest this new life with the very attribute of death--that of fell and malignant tyranny, of which we were the hapless victims. Nor does he say Life reigns in us, which would have been a scriptural enough idea; but, which is much more pregnant, "We shall reign in life." While freedom and might are implied in the figure of "reigning," "life" is represented as the glorious territory or atmosphere of that reign. And by recurring to the idea of <reference osisRef="Rom.5.16">Ro 5:16</reference>, as to the "many offenses" whose complete pardon shows "the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness," the whole statement is to this effect: "If one man's one offense let loose against us the tyrant power of Death, to hold us as its victims in helpless bondage, 'much more,' when we stand forth enriched with God's 'abounding grace' and in the beauty of a complete absolution from countless offenses, shall we expatiate in a life divinely owned and legally secured, 'reigning' in exultant freedom and unchallenged might, through that other matchless 'One,' Jesus Christ!" (On the import of the future tense in this last clause, see on <reference osisRef="Rom.5.19">Ro 5:19</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Rom.6.5">Ro 6:5</reference>). <div eID="gen31956" type="x-p"/>
entries.46d55e26ac9c3a63fc9be99eebdc7b0672d8a1e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16449"/><div sID="gen31957" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16449"/><hi type="bold">18. Therefore--</hi>now at length resuming the unfinished comparison of <reference osisRef="Rom.5.12">Ro 5:12</reference>, in order to give formally the concluding member of it, which had been done once and again substantially, in the intermediate verses.<div eID="gen31957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31958" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as by the offence of one judgment came--</hi>or, more simply, "it came."<div eID="gen31958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31959" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon all men to condenmation; even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came--</hi>rather, "it came."<div eID="gen31959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31960" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon all men to justification of life--</hi>(So Calvin, Bengel, Olshausen, Tholuck, Hodge, Philippi). But better, as we judge: "As through one offense it [came] upon all men to condemnation; even so through one righteousness [it came] upon all men to justification of life"--(So Beza, Grotius, Ferme, Meyer, De Wette, Alford, Revised Version). In this case, the apostle, resuming the statement of <reference osisRef="Rom.5.12">Ro 5:12</reference>, expresses it in a more concentrated and vivid form--suggested no doubt by the expression in <reference osisRef="Rom.5.16">Ro 5:16</reference>, "through one offense," representing Christ's whole work, considered as the ground of our justification, as "ONE RIGHTEOUSNESS." (Some would render the peculiar word here employed, "one righteous act" [Alford, &c.]; understanding by it Christ's death as the one redeeming act which reversed the one undoing act of Adam. But this is to limit the apostle's idea too much; for as the same word is properly rendered "righteousness" in <reference osisRef="Rom.8.4">Ro 8:4</reference>, where it means "the righteousness of the law as fulfilled by us who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit," so here it denotes Christ's whole "obedience unto death," considered as the one meritorious ground of the reversal of the condemnation which came by Adam. But on this, and on the expression, "all men," see on <reference osisRef="Rom.5.19">Ro 5:19</reference>. The expression "justification of life," is a vivid combination of two ideas already expatiated upon, meaning "justification entitling to and issuing in the rightful possession and enjoyment of life"). <div eID="gen31960" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd4514ef0fdf0033258a1c33da856327d6b433cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16450"/><div sID="gen31961" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16450"/><hi type="bold">19. For, &c.--</hi>better, "For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, even so by the obedience of the One shall the many be made righteous." On this great verse observe: First, By the "obedience" of Christ here is plainly not meant more than what divines call His active obedience, as distinguished from His sufferings and death; it is the entire work of Christ in its obediential character. Our Lord Himself represents even His death as His great act of obedience to the Father: "This commandment (that is, to lay down and resume His life) have I received of My Father" (<reference osisRef="John.10.8">Joh 10:8</reference>). Second, The significant word twice rendered made, does not signify to work a change upon a person or thing, but to constitute or ordain, as will be seen from all the places where it is used. Here, accordingly, it is intended to express that judicial act which holds men, in virtue of their connection with Adam, as sinners; and, in connection with Christ, as righteous. Third, The change of tense from the past to the future--"as through Adam we were made sinners, so through Christ we shall be made righteous"--delightfully expresses the enduring character of the act, and of the economy to which such acts belong, in contrast with the for-ever-past ruin of believers in Adam. (See on <reference osisRef="Rom.6.5">Ro 6:5</reference>). Fourth, The "all men" of <reference osisRef="Rom.5.18">Ro 5:18</reference> and the "many" of <reference osisRef="Rom.5.19">Ro 5:19</reference> are the same party, though under a slightly different aspect. In the latter case, the contrast is between the one representative (Adam--Christ) and the many whom he represented; in the former case, it is between the one head (Adam--Christ) and the human race, affected for death and life respectively by the actings of that one. Only in this latter case it is the redeemed family of man that is alone in view; it is humanity as actually lost, but also as actually saved, as ruined and recovered. Such as refuse to fall in with the high purpose of God to constitute His Son a "second Adam," the Head of a new race, and as impenitent and unbelieving finally perish, have no place in this section of the Epistle, whose sole object is to show how God repairs in the second Adam the evil done by the first. (Thus the doctrine of universal restoration has no place here. Thus too the forced interpretation by which the "justification of all" is made to mean a justification merely in possibility and offer to all, and the "justification of the many" to mean the actual justification of as many as believe [Alford, &c.], is completely avoided. And thus the harshness of comparing a whole fallen family with a recovered part is got rid of. However true it be in fact that part of mankind is not saved, this is not the aspect in which the subject is here presented. It is totals that are compared and contrasted; and it is the same total in two successive conditions--namely, the human race as ruined in Adam and recovered in Christ). <div eID="gen31961" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a56581ef3fc706ab46855c1787e78dc9f4a4586: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16451"/><div sID="gen31962" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16451"/><hi type="bold">20-21. Moreover the law--</hi>"The law, however." The Jew might say, If the whole purposes of God towards men center in Adam and Christ, where does "the law" come in, and what was the use of it? Answer: It<div eID="gen31962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">entered--</hi>But the word expresses an important idea besides "entering." It signifies, "entered incidentally," or "parenthetically." (In <reference osisRef="Gal.2.4">Ga 2:4</reference> <hi type="bold">the same word is rendered, "came in privily.") The meaning is, that the promulgation of the law at Sinai was no primary or essential feature of the divine plan, but it was "added" (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.19">Ga 3:19</reference>) for a subordinate purpose--</hi>the more fully to reveal the evil occasioned by Adam, and the need and glory of the remedy by Christ.<div eID="gen31963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31964" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that the offence might abound--</hi>or, "be multiplied." But what offense? Throughout all this section "the offense" (four times repeated besides here) has one definite meaning, namely, "the one first offense of Adam"; and this, in our judgment, is its meaning here also: "All our multitudinous breaches of the law are nothing but that one first offense, lodged mysteriously in the bosom of every child of Adam as an offending principal, and multiplying itself into myriads of particular offenses in the life of each." What was one act of disobedience in the head has been converted into a vital and virulent principle of disobedience in all the members of the human family, whose every act of wilful rebellion proclaims itself the child of the original transgression.<div eID="gen31964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">But where sin abounded--</hi>or, "was multiplied."<div eID="gen31965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31966" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grace did much more abound--</hi>rather, "did exceedingly abound," or "superabound." The comparison here is between the multiplication of one offense into countless transgressions, and such an overflow of grace as more than meets that appalling case. <div eID="gen31966" type="x-p"/>

entries.9f8b9e122e8a91be369f81fde55cfa0860e61780: <div eID="gen46175" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen46176" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen46177" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen46177" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen46176" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen46178" type="x-p"/> The effects of justification by faith, peace with God, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.1">Rom 5:1</reference>. The joyous hope of eternal glory, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.2">Rom 5:2</reference>. Glorying in tribulations, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.3">Rom 5:3</reference>. And gaining thereby patience, experience, and hope, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.4">Rom 5:4</reference>. And having the love of God shed abroad in the heart by the Holy Spirit, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">Rom 5:5</reference>. The state of the world when Christ died for it, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.6-Rom.5.10">Rom 5:6-10</reference>. Jesus Christ is an atonement, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.11">Rom 5:11</reference>. Sin and death entered into the world by Adam's transgression, and all became guilty before God, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.12-Rom.5.14">Rom 5:12-14</reference>. God's grace in sending Christ into the world to save fallen man, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.15-Rom.5.19">Rom 5:15-19</reference>. The law is brought in to show the exceeding sinfulness of sin, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.20">Rom 5:20</reference>.
